name: Heureka Science Centre
sub: The best children's museum in Finland
desc: A hands-on science centre: a paper mill you can operate, a lie detector, a giant pendulum, rats playing basketball, and a planetarium.
why: For a 9- and a 7-year-old this beats every castle in Europe. Everything can be touched, and it is 15 minutes off the Helsinki–Tampere motorway.
tip: Buy online the night before — €3 per person cheaper and you skip the queue. Under-5s free. Lockers by the entrance; picnic room downstairs if you bring lunch.

name: Korkeasaari Zoo
sub: Island zoo, reached by ferry
desc: A zoo on its own island east of the centre: snow leopards, bears, lynx, and a farm yard of Finnish animals, reached by a short ferry or bus.
why: Real animals in a cold Nordic setting — the snow leopards are more active in November than in summer.
tip: Winter closing is 16:00 and the last entry is an hour before. The HSL day ticket covers the ferry.

name: Suomenlinna Fortress
sub: Sea fortress on six islands
desc: A UNESCO-listed 18th-century sea fortress spread over islands, with ramparts, tunnels, cannons, a submarine and a toy museum.
why: Children can climb walls and disappear into tunnels legally, and the ferry is part of the fun. Free to enter.
tip: Take the HSL ferry from the Market Square (10.60 adult day ticket, under-7s free). Windy and exposed — full waterproofs. Café Piper and the brewery are the warm stops.

name: Oodi Central Library
sub: Finland's living room, free
desc: A spectacular timber-and-glass library opposite the parliament: a children's floor with a storybook forest, 3D printers, sewing machines and a cinema.
why: Free, warm, central, and the children's section is genuinely one of the best in Europe. Rated 4.8 by 20,000 people.
tip: Third floor is the quiet reading room; second floor is where the children and the noise are. Free toilets and lockers.

name: Natural History Museum
sub: A moose, a mammoth and 13 million specimens
desc: Helsinki's natural history museum in a 1913 building: a full moose, a mammoth skeleton, dinosaurs, and a hall of Finnish nature.
why: The right size for two hours, entirely indoor, and the animal halls work for a 9-month-old as well as a 9-year-old.
tip: Enter from Kaisaniemi park. Monday closed — plan it for Saturday.

name: Market Square & Old Market Hall
sub: Salmon soup on the harbour
desc: The harbour market in front of the cathedral, with salmon soup, fried vendace, berries and coffee, plus the 1889 brick market hall behind it.
why: A cheap hot lunch with a view of the ferries — and the only place where the children can see the fish being cooked in front of them.
tip: Salmon soup (lohikeitto) with rye bread is €10–14 and fills an adult. Cash for the stalls. Windy — eat inside the hall if it rains.

name: Helsinki Cathedral
sub: The white cathedral on Senate Square
desc: Carl Ludvig Engel's 1852 cathedral, raised above Senate Square with a flight of steps that functions as the city's front porch.
why: The steps are the attraction: run up, look down at the square, and it is free. Two minutes from the market.
tip: Climb the steps for the photo, go inside for the warmth. Services closed to tourists on Sunday mornings.

name: Temppeliaukio Rock Church
sub: A church blasted into granite
desc: A 1969 church excavated from solid rock, with a copper dome, raw stone walls and extraordinary acoustics.
why: It takes 20 minutes and looks like nothing else on the trip. Children understand 'they blew a hole in a rock and put a roof on it'.
tip: Entry fee applies in tourist hours. Check for concert times — a 15-minute organ rehearsal is better than the visit itself.

name: Sea Life Helsinki
sub: Aquarium next to Linnanmäki
desc: An indoor aquarium with sharks, rays, a tunnel tank and Baltic Sea species, aimed squarely at families.
why: Warm, dark and calming — the best 90 minutes in Helsinki when it is raining and everyone is over museums.
tip: Expensive for what it is; book online for a discount. Combine with the Linnanmäki area, which is free to walk even when the rides are shut.

name: Linnanmäki
sub: Amusement park — closed for the season
desc: Helsinki's hilltop amusement park, open from late April to October, with a wooden roller coaster from 1951.
why: Listed so nobody promises the children a theme park on the way home: the season ends in October.
tip: Skip. Sea Life next door stays open all year.

name: Finnish Aviation Museum
sub: Planes you can walk under, by the airport
desc: A hangar of Finnish aviation history next to Helsinki-Vantaa airport: fighters, a DC-3, engines, and cockpits to climb into.
why: Only 5 minutes from the airport — the perfect stop if you have time before a flight, or a rainy-hour alternative to Heureka.
tip: Climbing into the cockpits is the whole point for children. Cold hangars — keep coats on.

name: Tallinn Old Town
sub: Medieval walls, towers, marzipan
desc: A UNESCO-listed Hanseatic old town: the town hall square, 14th-century walls, round towers, and the oldest continuously operating pharmacy in Europe.
why: A genuine fairy-tale city, and familiar ground for Lithuanians — cheap, close, and easy to walk with a buggy except on the cobbles.
tip: Cobblestones are brutal with a buggy — take the carrier and let the 9-year-old push the empty pram. Climb the town hall tower (€5) if it is open.

name: Seaplane Harbour (Lennusadam)
sub: A submarine you can walk inside
desc: A vast 1917 seaplane hangar holding the submarine Lembit, a mine, seaplanes, and interactive displays on the Baltic.
why: Rated 4.8 — the best museum in the Baltics for children. You can go inside a real submarine, and the hangar is warm and enormous.
tip: Family ticket €40 covers everything including the museum ships. Monday closed. 15 minutes' walk from the Old Town through Kalamaja.

name: PROTO Invention Factory
sub: VR and 19th-century inventions
desc: An interactive museum in the old Noblessner shipyard where you fly a da Vinci machine, ride a steam train and dive in a submarine, mostly in VR.
why: Aimed exactly at 7–12 year olds, indoors, and a family ticket covers all five. The 9-month-old will not participate.
tip: VR headsets have a minimum age — the 7-year-old may need an adult. Book a slot online at weekends. Under-6s free.

name: Tallinn Zoo
sub: Big zoo, 15 min from the centre
desc: One of the largest zoos in the Baltics, with elephants, big cats, a tropical house and a large collection of Nordic animals.
why: The tropical house is warm and indoor — a good November stop — and the 7-year-old can walk the whole loop.
tip: Large site, 3 km of walking; take the buggy. Winter closing 17:00, last entry 16:00.

name: Tallinn TV Tower
sub: 175 m, glass floor, Baltic view
desc: A 314-metre Soviet-era broadcast tower with a 175-metre observation deck, a glass floor section, and a café.
why: Clear-day views over Tallinn, forest and sea, plus the mild terror of the glass floor — a guaranteed 9-year-old highlight.
tip: Check visibility before going up; on a grey day you see fog. The glass floor is optional — there is a solid path around it.

name: Kadriorg Park & KUMU
sub: Palace park, playground, art museum
desc: Peter the Great's baroque palace park with fountains, a swan pond, a large playground, and KUMU, the Estonian art museum.
why: The best free park in Tallinn: flat paths, a proper playground, and a café in the palace kitchen.
tip: The playground is behind the palace. Skip KUMU with children unless it is raining hard.

name: Pirita Beach & Promenade
sub: Pine forest to the sea
desc: Tallinn's seaside district: a long sandy beach backed by pine forest, with a promenade and the ruins of St Bridget's convent.
why: A proper beach walk 15 minutes from the centre — sand, pine smell, and space to run after a long car day.
tip: In November it is a walk, not a swim — windproof layers. Free parking along the promenade in winter.

name: Balti Jaama Market
sub: Three floors of cheap food
desc: A refurbished market next to the railway station: street-food counters, a butcher, a bakery, a fish hall and a supermarket downstairs.
why: The cheapest good lunch in Tallinn, indoors, with something for every child and a supermarket for the car.
tip: Go up to the street-food floor. Buy bread, cheese and fruit downstairs for the drive.

name: Telliskivi Creative City
sub: Old railway workshops, now food and murals
desc: A former railway repair yard turned into a district of street art, small shops, food trucks and the Fotografiska museum.
why: Between the Old Town and the Seaplane Harbour, so it is a natural lunch stop on the walk — and children like the trains and the murals.
tip: Weekend food trucks are best. The Depoo street-food hall is indoors and cheap.

name: Pärnu Beach & Promenade
sub: Estonia's summer capital, empty in November
desc: A long white-sand beach with a promenade, playgrounds, a pier and pine park, on the route between Tallinn and Riga.
why: The best leg-stretch on the whole drive home: 8 minutes off the main road, free, with a playground and toilets.
tip: Park at the Ranna parkla. In November everything is closed except a few cafés — bring a thermos.

name: Tervise Paradiis Water Park
sub: Indoor water park on the beach
desc: Estonia's biggest indoor water park: slides, a wave pool, a children's pool, saunas, attached to a spa hotel on Pärnu beach.
why: The single best rainy-day stop on the drive home, and a hotel attached if you want to break the journey.
tip: Book online; family tickets are cheaper. Bring own towels. Slides have height limits — the 7-year-old may need the small ones.

name: Riga Old Town
sub: Art nouveau, markets and the Christmas tree
desc: The Hanseatic old town: the Town Hall Square, the House of the Blackheads, St Peter's church tower, and the Central Market in five zeppelin hangars.
why: A natural lunch and leg-stretch stop on the Riga bypass, and St Peter's tower has a lift to the top.
tip: Park under the Central Market (free for 2 h with purchase). The market hangars are the cheapest lunch in the Baltics.

name: Riga Zoo
sub: Big, green, 20 min from the centre
desc: A large zoo in the forested Mežaparks district, with a tropical house, elephants, and a children's zoo with goats.
why: Worth a half-day detour if you overnight in Riga — the children's zoo is hands-on and the site is flat.
tip: Winter hours 10–17. Combine with Mežaparks forest and the nearby Līvu water park.

name: Līvu Akvaparks
sub: Water slides in Jūrmala
desc: One of the biggest indoor water parks in northern Europe, 20 minutes west of Riga, with slides, a wave pool, saunas and a kids' zone.
why: If you overnight between Tallinn and Vilnius, this is the stop that makes the drive feel like a holiday rather than a transfer.
tip: Book online, bring towels and flip-flops. Height limits on the big slides; the baby area is warm and shallow.

name: Riga Motor Museum
sub: Cars behind the Iron Curtain
desc: A modern museum of vehicles, including the limousines of Soviet leaders and a hall of Baltic motorsport, with interactive displays.
why: Warm, indoor, and full of cars — a reliable hour for children on a cold day in Riga.
tip: Right by the Riga bypass, so it works as a driving break without entering the city.

name: Latvian Ethnographic Open-Air Museum
sub: A village in the forest by the lake
desc: A large forest park of 100+ relocated farmsteads, churches and windmills from across Latvia, on the shore of Lake Jugla.
why: Cheap, spacious and full of wooden houses to peek into; children can run between them.
tip: Gravel paths — carrier rather than buggy. Some houses closed in winter; the walk is still good.

name: Sigulda & Gutmanis Cave
sub: Gauja valley, castles, bobsleigh
desc: The Gauja river valley: red sandstone cliffs, Gutmanis cave with its 17th-century inscriptions, two castles, and a bobsleigh track.
why: The most scenic hour of the whole drive home, an hour from Riga, and free apart from the castles.
tip: The cave is 5 minutes from the car park. Turaida castle is a 3 km walk or a short drive. Steep paths — carrier.

name: Cēsis Castle
sub: Livonian Order ruins and a new castle
desc: Ruins of a 13th-century Livonian Order castle beside a 19th-century manor, with towers to climb and cellars to explore.
why: Romantic ruins without the crowds of Sigulda, and a pretty small town for lunch.
tip: The west tower has the best view; stairs are narrow. Closed Mondays in winter.

name: Rundāle Palace
sub: The Baltic Versailles, 80 km from Riga
desc: Bartolomeo Rastrelli's baroque palace for the Dukes of Courland, with gilded state rooms and a formal French garden.
why: The most impressive interior in the Baltics and only 20 minutes from the Lithuanian border route — a good final-day stop.
tip: The garden is free-ish and better for children than the state rooms. Café on site. Bauska castle is 12 km away.

name: Bauska Castle
sub: Ruined fortress at the river confluence
desc: The ruins of a 15th-century Livonian castle on a spit between two rivers, with a small museum and views from the tower.
why: Fifteen minutes off the Via Baltica, cheap, and quick — a good 60-minute break with real castle walls to touch.
tip: Short visit only; the tower climb is the highlight. Combine with Rundāle if you have the day.

name: Hill of Crosses
sub: Thousands of crosses on a hill
desc: A small hill covered in tens of thousands of crosses left by pilgrims, 12 km north of Šiauliai.
why: Fifteen minutes off the Via Baltica and unlike anything else: silent, strange, and free. A good last stop before home.
tip: Free parking 300 m away. Paths are gravel — buggy works. Bring a small cross if you want to leave one.

name: Trakai Island Castle
sub: A castle in the middle of a lake
desc: A 14th-century Gothic castle on an island in Lake Galvė, reached by a wooden footbridge, with a museum of Lithuanian history inside.
why: The best castle in Lithuania and 30 minutes from Vilnius — the obvious 'we are nearly home' reward for the children.
tip: Footbridge is 300 m — buggy possible but cobbled. Karaim pasties (kibinai) in the village are the local food; buy a bag for the car.

name: Vilnius Old Town
sub: Home
desc: The largest surviving medieval old town in the Baltics, and the end of the drive.
why: An anchor on the map so you can see the shape of the whole loop: Vilnius → Tallinn → Tampere → Tallinn → Vilnius.
tip: After 1,600 km in nine days, the last thing anyone needs is a walking tour. Go home.
